narrative.text: A blank page with no extracted text.
The copyright notice for a 1995 WHO document, stating that it is not a formal publication but may be freely reviewed, reproduced or translated for non-commercial use.

The first page of the table of contents of WHO's 1995 guidelines on counselling for HIV/AIDS, listing the preface, acknowledgements, introduction and early sections; the extracted text contains OCR noise in the dot leaders.

Continues the table of contents of the HIV/AIDS counselling guidelines, listing sections on providers, training, integration with health services, links with other services, monitoring and evaluation, figures and annexes, with some OCR noise.

The preface to 'Counselling for HIV/AIDS: a key to caring', recalling WHO's 1990 counselling guidelines in the AIDS series and explaining how understanding of counselling has developed since. It describes counselling as listening and talking with people about how HIV/AIDS affects them, in many settings.

Acknowledges the independent consultant who contributed to the counselling guidelines and the people living with AIDS, care-givers and service managers whose work informed them. It also lists reviewers and contributors from organizations in several countries.

Introduces the guidelines, explaining that they are intended for policy-makers and planners in health and social services to help them develop policies supporting HIV/AIDS counselling services. It notes they may also interest managers and clinicians involved in policy-making.

Lists policy issues the guidelines address, such as defining who qualifies as a counsellor and preparing staff for a new activity. It outlines the document's structure and refers to related WHO/GPA publications.

Opens Part One by giving the Global Programme on AIDS definition of HIV/AIDS counselling as a confidential dialogue that helps clients cope with stress and make personal decisions. It describes the components, including personal risk assessment and planning to reduce risk.

Lists those who should receive HIV/AIDS counselling, including people with AIDS or HIV and their families, people seeking an HIV test and those worried about their risk. It also identifies others who may be involved, such as partners, household members and wider family.

Tells the story of a man who sought an HIV test and was counselled by a nurse about his sexual history, fears and the test, illustrating pre-test counselling. It explains the window period when people are infectious but test antibody negative.

Continues the case story, describing how the man learned his positive result and was helped through role-play to tell his wife. Over the following years he and his wife received ongoing supportive counselling and social support.

Continues the case story with home-based care, emotional support from care teams, hospital care and spiritual support. It describes how the man told colleagues about his status and educated them about HIV, changing their attitudes.

Concludes the case story with workplace social support and home-based counselling for the couple. It then begins describing the components of counselling, including information on reducing HIV risk through abstinence, fidelity and condoms.

Continues the components of counselling, including advice on condoms and reducing partners, and explains that the emphasis of each session depends on the client's needs. It stresses confidentiality and not disclosing results to third parties without explicit consent.

Describes counselling as a responsive, empowering dialogue rather than a didactic process, and contrasts it with health education. It lists related activities such as care for patients worried about infection and community education.

A figure showing the relative emphasis of emotional support, information-giving and risk reduction across a series of counselling sessions, following the case story from testing to illness and death; the extracted text is fragmentary.
Summarizes Part One, describing HIV/AIDS counselling as a confidential dialogue offering emotional support, risk assessment and information, distinct from health education.

Opens Part Two on policy issues, explaining that counselling services aim to meet the emotional support needs of people with HIV-related concerns. It stresses the need for policies that support counselling as part of wider HIV/AIDS activities.

Lists local factors planners should consider when developing counselling policies. It explains how counselling and education reinforce each other by making messages more personally relevant and helping overcome emotional barriers to change.

Explains how education raises awareness of counselling services and how counselling links with clinical care. It lists sites where counselling should be available, such as antenatal and STD clinics, HIV care settings and testing sites.

Lists additional sites for counselling in high-prevalence areas, such as community support settings, workplace clinics and voluntary testing centres. It notes that counsellors must understand the cultures of the groups they serve.

Lists the range of people who may provide HIV/AIDS counselling, from specially trained nurses and social workers to specialist counsellors, community members and volunteers. It introduces a figure showing how providers vary between settings.

The extracted text of this page is garbled OCR of rotated or mirrored text; it appears to be Figure 2, showing categories of counselling providers by level of training and social distance from the client.

Describes how counselling is commonly provided by trained nurses and social workers, with specialist counsellors for referral, and discusses peer and volunteer counsellors. It also covers telephone counselling, which needs counsellors with further training.

Discourages giving HIV test results by telephone and describes an AIDS hotline example in which a young man named Peter receives anonymous counselling. It then discusses counsellor training, stressing supervised practical experience.

Refers to the GPA Source Book for HIV/AIDS Counselling Training as material for adapting training courses, and discusses supervision and support for counsellors. It notes that supplementary materials should be integrated into counselling by a trained counsellor.

Recommends written procedures for organizing counselling services to support supervision and referral, and discusses integrating counselling into existing health services. It gives examples of referral, such as a woman with HIV referred to family planning services.

Describes Zambia's national approach to scaling up HIV/AIDS counselling through existing health and social workers. Measures include a national focal point, training and supervision, and counselling courses at higher education institutions.

Describes HIV counselling services in Myanmar, where HIV is concentrated among people who inject drugs and sex workers. Services began with follow-up of infected blood donors and expanded through trained counsellors who train others.

Lists further services that counselling links with, such as blood transfusion services where pre-donation counselling helps high-risk donors defer. It also mentions referrals to community groups and to religious workers for spiritual needs.

The extracted text of this page is garbled OCR of rotated or mirrored text; it appears to be Figure 3, showing the HIV/AIDS continuum of care linking hospitals, community and home-based care, counselling and testing, blood transfusion services and self-help groups.

Explains that voluntary HIV testing should be part of a comprehensive counselling programme with pre-test and post-test counselling and support services. It begins discussing monitoring and evaluation of counselling services, including policy statements.

Lists further elements for evaluating counselling services, such as procedures, standards and monitoring criteria. It then turns to special situations, including counselling on infant feeding for mothers with HIV and the risks of bottle-feeding.

Notes that where clean water is lacking, bottle-feeding may carry a greater risk of death than breastfeeding by a mother with HIV, and refers to GPA guidance on infant feeding policy. It then discusses counselling young people and understanding their culture.

Continues on counselling young people, then describes special problems in counselling adolescents with haemophilia and their families, such as maternal guilt over inherited disease and contaminated blood products. It begins an example family counselling dialogue with a boy named Peter.

Continues the example dialogue in which a counsellor explores worries within a family of an adolescent with haemophilia and HIV. The dialogue is drawn from a published text on systematic HIV counselling.

Summarises a 1992 WHO consultation on HIV testing, which warned that testing without informed consent harms prevention while voluntary testing with counselling can support both seropositive and seronegative people. It then considers how future developments, such as new testing products and better clinical care prolonging life, could raise demand for HIV/AIDS counselling.
Notes that large HIV vaccine trials will increase demand for counselling and that trial protocols and national planners should provide for counselling services and training.

Summarises Part Two of the guide, stating that HIV/AIDS counselling helps people cope with infection and testing, should be linked to other HIV activities and integrated into existing services, and is usually delivered by staff with in-service counselling training.

Opens Part Three on the role of policy-makers and planners, listing policies needed before counselling services start, such as clear objectives, confidential or anonymous testing procedures, voluntary testing with informed consent and rules on who provides counselling. It stresses that policy-makers can play a key role and that a review of existing policies may be needed.

Sets out seven steps for developing HIV/AIDS counselling policy, from naming a coordinator and identifying issues through drafting, review, dissemination and monitoring. It describes the first step, including who should take part in the policy process, such as AIDS committee members, planners, service providers, clinicians and NGOs.

Describes the coordinator's situation report on epidemiology, demand and existing counselling services and training, with supporting documents. It explains how priority policy issues may differ between high-prevalence settings, where staffing matters most, and low-prevalence settings, where confidentiality and partner notification may dominate.

Explains how participants rank policy issues to select five or six priorities and how each is analysed, with examples of general and specific policies and the means to implement them, such as legislation. It notes that written policies are then drafted, though implicit policies may be used where public opposition delays formal ones.

Describes the final steps of policy development: review and approval by senior officials, wide dissemination with any retraining and sensitization of staff at counselling sites, and monitoring of implementation. It refers to an example of a national policy statement in Box 6.

Notes that managers need detailed technical guidelines on counselling services and training and lists WHO/GPA materials on topics such as setting up services, training counsellors, blood transfusion services and breast-feeding advice for HIV-positive mothers. It summarises the importance of developing policies through wide consultation.

Presents Kenya's 1988 Ministry of Health policy statement on AIDS counselling, covering training of all health workers, family-centred counselling, district plans, confidentiality and protection from dismissal because of HIV status.
Lists WHO/GPA materials on HIV/AIDS counselling and related areas, grouped under testing, training, clinical management and care, and counselling service delivery.

Opens the glossary of the counselling guide, defining client, counselling, pre-test and post-test counselling and types of testing. It distinguishes anonymous and confidential testing and testing initiated by clients, health care providers or third parties.

Continues the glossary, defining testing with and without informed consent, voluntary testing and mandatory testing. It advises against the term 'routine testing' because it does not say whether informed consent is sought.
